title: Parenting Style Quiz
description: Discover your natural parenting style — covering eight recognized styles from developmental psychology and modern parenting culture: authoritative, authoritarian, permissive, uninvolved, helicopter, positive parenting, free-range, and attachment.

scoring.method: sum points per style tag, highest total = dominant parenting style, second-highest = secondary tendency

authoritative.title: Authoritative
authoritative.description: High warmth, high structure. You set clear expectations and follow through, while staying responsive to your child's feelings and perspective. Widely regarded by researchers as the style most associated with confident, resilient kids.
strengths: raises kids who understand the "why" behind rules
growthEdges: can be exhausting to maintain consistently
watch for over-explaining when a simple limit would do
tips: Keep pairing limits with a brief reason — it's working, keep doing it
On hard days, a short firm boundary is still fine; you don't have to fully explain every single time
Model how you want conflict handled — your calm follow-through is the biggest teacher here

authoritarian.title: Authoritarian
authoritarian.description: High structure, lower warmth in the moment. You value obedience, consistency, and clear rules — strong on structure, but the connection side may need more room.
growthEdges: making space for your child's perspective before deciding
softening tone during correction
praising effort, not just compliance
tips: Try asking "what happened?" before jumping to the consequence — it often changes nothing about the outcome, but changes everything about how it lands
Add one specific praise for effort or character each day, not just correction
Explain the reason behind a rule once in a while — even a one-sentence "because..." builds trust without losing authority

permissive.title: Permissive
permissive.description: High warmth, lower structure. You're warm, responsive, and avoid unnecessary conflict — the connection is strong, but limits may not stick.
growthEdges: following through on stated consequences
tolerating short-term pushback for long-term structure
saying no without guilt
tips: Pick one or two rules to enforce consistently this month rather than trying to fix everything at once
A boundary held calmly, even through a tantrum, teaches more than a warning that doesn't stick
Remember: saying no to a request isn't withholding love — kids feel safer with real limits, even when they protest them

uninvolved.title: Uninvolved
uninvolved.description: Lower warmth, lower structure — often not by choice, but a sign of a season where bandwidth is stretched thin (work stress, personal struggles, too many demands at once).
growthEdges: carving out small, regular one-on-one time
re-engaging with school and daily routines
noticing what's making consistent presence hard right now
tips: Start small — even 10 minutes of undistracted time daily rebuilds connection faster than one big gesture
If this result surprises or concerns you, it's worth being honest with yourself about what's making presence hard right now — work, stress, or something else — and whether outside support would help
One consistent routine (like a nightly check-in) can rebuild structure without needing to overhaul everything at once

helicopter.title: Helicopter
helicopter.description: High involvement, low room for struggle. You're deeply invested and quick to step in — your child rarely faces a problem alone, though that same closeness can crowd out the space they need to build confidence on their own.
strengths: quick to notice when something's wrong
growthEdges: letting small struggles play out before stepping in
resisting the urge to fix things that aren't truly urgent
building your child's confidence in solving things solo
tips: Before stepping in, pause and ask "is this actually unsafe, or just uncomfortable to watch?" — most struggles are the second one
Let a small mistake stand sometimes — a forgotten lunch or a lost point teaches more than a rescue does
Try narrating confidence instead of taking over: "I think you can figure this one out" builds more than doing it for them

positive.title: Positive Parenting
positive.description: High warmth, high structure, low punishment. You lead with empathy and hold firm boundaries at the same time — focused on teaching the skill behind the behavior, not just stopping it.
growthEdges: can take more patience and energy than a quick punishment
watch for boundaries softening under pushback
staying consistent when you're exhausted
tips: Name the feeling before addressing the behavior — "you're really frustrated, and also, hitting isn't okay" does both jobs at once
A boundary can be calm and firm at the same time — you don't need anger to make a limit stick
When you lose your cool, a short repair afterward ("I raised my voice, I'm sorry, let's try again") models more than getting it perfect

freerange.title: Free-range
freerange.description: High independence, lower supervision. You trust your child with real responsibility and room to make mistakes — building resilience and problem-solving, sometimes ahead of what feels comfortable to others.
strengths: comfortable letting kids learn from natural consequences
growthEdges: checking that freedom still matches your child's actual readiness, not just their age
staying available without hovering when they do need you
explaining your reasoning to family or caregivers who worry
tips: Match the freedom to the child, not the calendar — readiness varies a lot between kids the same age
"I trust you to handle this, and I'm nearby if you need me" gives independence without disappearing
A quick check-in before a new freedom (routes, plans, what to do if lost) sets them up to succeed at it

attachment.title: Attachment
attachment.description: High closeness, high responsiveness. You prioritize physical bonding and quick responses to your child's needs — built on the idea that a secure early bond is the foundation everything else grows from.
growthEdges: making space for structure and independence as your child grows older
protecting your own rest and bandwidth
letting go a little as needs shift from infancy to childhood
tips: Responsiveness matters at every age, but what it looks like should grow with your child — comfort a toddler differently than you comforted a newborn
Your own rest isn't optional — a depleted parent struggles to stay as attuned as this style asks for
As your child grows, gradually introduced independence doesn't undo the bond you've built — it's built on top of it
